Magnanimous

mag-NAN-uh-muhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Magnanimous is very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone with less power.

The outgoing mayor was magnanimous during the concession speech, thanking the voters who had chosen someone else.

Worked Example

Though he'd caught his rival cheating on the exam, the magnanimous student chose to warn him privately instead of reporting him.

He had every right to be harsh, but chose generosity and forgiveness instead, which is exactly the quality magnanimous names.

How Strong Is It? — polite → self-sacrificing → magnanimous

polite vs. magnanimous

self-sacrificing vs. magnanimous

self-sacrificing vs. magnanimous: willing to give up one's own interests for others

Build the Word

The pieces

root — magn-

root — magn-: great (also seen in magnitude and magnify) (Latin magnus)

root — anim-

root — anim-: mind, spirit, soul (Latin animus)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Magnanimous joins Latin magnus ('great') and animus ('mind, spirit') plus -ous, 'full of' -- literally 'full of great-spiritedness.' A magnanimous person has a spirit too great to be small or petty, even in victory.

Word Choice

Magnanimous is often paired with victory or an advantage -- it's generosity shown specifically from a position of strength, toward someone who has less power in the moment.
